title: Linear-time exact inversion counting
formal: Do there exist one uniform deterministic word-RAM algorithm \(A\) and a constant \(C>0\) such that, for every \(n\ge2\) and every explicitly listed permutation \(\pi\) of \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), \(A\) outputs \[\operatorname{Inv}(\pi)=|\{(i,j)\in[n]^2:i<j\ \text{and}\ \pi(i)>\pi(j)\}|\] exactly, using at most \(Cn\) machine instructions in the worst case? The word length and allowed instructions are specified below. The constant and the program must be independent of \(n\) and \(\pi\).
definitions: The input contains \(n\) and the array \(\pi(1),\ldots,\pi(n)\), promised to contain each integer from one through \(n\) exactly once. The output is the single integer inversion count, between zero and \(n(n-1)/2\). Use a uniform word RAM with word length \(w=d\lceil\log_{2}(n+2)\rceil\), for a fixed positive integer \(d\) chosen with the algorithm and large enough for its addresses and input values. Unit-cost instructions are word reads/writes, copying, comparisons, branching, Boolean operations, shifts, addition, subtraction and multiplication modulo \(2^{w}\), and integer quotient and remainder with nonzero divisor. Shifts by at least \(w\) return zero. Multiword computation is charged by its component instructions. The fixed finite program receives no advice or precomputed tables; all initialization, preprocessing and output writes count. Choose \(d\ge3\), so the count fits in a word. All constants are independent of the permutation and \(n\). No randomness is allowed. The values are already ranks, so no conversion from arbitrary ordered keys is required. The array has one entry per word; no compressed representation, streaming restriction or comparison-only restriction is imposed. The algorithm may use auxiliary random-access memory, but allocating, initializing and accessing that memory consumes the counted steps. The output is one word containing the exact nonnegative integer. Neither a list of all inverted pairs nor individual per-position counts are required.

context_blocks.text: An inversion is a pair of positions whose values occur in decreasing order. Its total is the Kendall tau distance from the identity ordering and the minimum number of adjacent swaps required to sort the permutation.

Chan and Pătraşcu give a deterministic exact \(O(n\sqrt{\log_2 n})\)-time word-RAM algorithm. They also give a linear-time constant-relative-error approximation, which does not supply the exact output requested here.
Elmasry’s adaptive algorithm improves the time on inputs with fewer inversions, but retains a superlinear worst-case bound over all permutations.

Kempa and Kociumaka’s STOC 2025 paper again identifies inversion counting among the central problems whose fastest known algorithms have the square-root-logarithmic overhead. Theorem 1.3 transfers any improved inversion-counting time to a packed Dictionary Matching problem. Its bounded-integer array formulation and the permutation formulation have the same linear-time endpoint.

In that Dictionary Matching problem, the input consists of a packed binary text occupying a linear number of logarithmic-size words and a linear number of patterns, each of logarithmic bit length; the output says whether any pattern occurs. The connection is a conditional consequence for another task, not an unconditional superlinear lower bound. The linear exact endpoint remains the card’s explicit editorial formulation of the gap.

why: Exact inversion counting compresses a permutation’s pairwise disorder into one integer and is a fundamental offline aggregation task. Its complexity remains separated from the cost of sorting already rank-bounded integers. The 2025 hardness connections show that a linear-time solution would also change the algorithmic frontier for packed-string processing.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the existence assertion or its negation. A positive answer must specify one fixed program and prove its exact count and linear worst-case running time for every legal permutation in the specified model. A negative answer must exclude all such programs and all fixed constants. A relative-error estimate, an algorithm that is linear only on nearly sorted inputs, an expected-time randomized algorithm, or an improvement still superlinear in the worst case does not meet this target. A conditional lower bound establishes only its stated conditional implication.

progress.text: Chan–Pătraşcu publish exact \(O(n\sqrt{\log_2 n})\) counting and a linear-time relative approximation.
Elmasry posts an adaptive inversion-counting algorithm, with improved performance on low-inversion inputs.
Kempa–Kociumaka publish the Dictionary Matching hardness connection at STOC; their Theorem 1.3 transfers the inversion-counting running time to that task.

status_note: The checked STOC 2025 primary paper explicitly includes inversion counting among problems retaining an O(n sqrt(log n)) best-known word-RAM bound and proves a conditional connection to Dictionary Matching. Bounded later-work checks through 2026-09-15 found no exact deterministic linear-time algorithm or unconditional refutation. The linear endpoint is an editorial formulation of this documented gap, not an attributed named conjecture; the review is not an exhaustive proof of current openness.

sentences: An inversion is a pair of permutation positions whose values appear in decreasing order.
The task is to return the exact total number of such pairs as one integer.
The question asks whether one deterministic program can do this in linear worst-case time on a word RAM with logarithmic words.
Known approximation and adaptive algorithms do not provide that exact guarantee for every permutation.
A STOC 2025 result links faster exact inversion counting to faster packed Dictionary Matching, giving the question broader algorithmic significance.
